articles.title: Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in devastated Ukrainian city holds for its first 30 hours, officials say
articles.summary: Brokered by first lady Melania Trump, a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night, officials said.
articles.body: Brokered by first lady Melania Trump, a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night, officials said Wednesday, but Moscow and Kyiv continued to batter each other elsewhere. The localized truce in the devastated southern city of Oleshky began Tuesday and is due to last through Sunday as a planned humanitarian operation races to get its about 2,000 remaining residents urgently needed food and medicine, as well as evacuate those who want to leave. If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time since Russia’s invasion of its neighbor more than 4 ½ years ago that the two sides have observed a significant truce. Previous attempts to stop the fighting have either failed to take hold or quickly unraveled. Russia and Ukraine thank Melania Trump Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be sent to Oleshky before any evacuation corridors are opened. Russia’s occupying forces impose strict limits on who can enter Oleshky, and there was no news on how the humanitarian operation was unfolding. Russia’s ombudsperson Yana Lantratova and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsperson Dmytro Lubinets both said Wednesday there had been no ceasefire violations in Oleshky for 30 hours. The plight of the city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region caught the attention of Melania Trump, and the White House said she brokered the humanitarian mission. Pope Leo XIV also spoke this month with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said. Both Ukrainian and Russian officials, eager to win President Donald Trump’s approval as he pushes for an elusive peace settlement, thanked Melania Trump for her role. Zelenskyy said he was grateful to Melania Trump for her role in halting the fighting in and around Oleshky, where she says humanitarian corridors are being established to take people out. “We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine was ready to receive evacuees from the town. “Her personal involvement is of great importance to the entire process,” Russia’s Lantratova said. U.S. awaits Middle East events The ceasefire coincided with U.S.-led plans to bring Moscow and Kyiv officials back to the table next month for technical talks on how to move forward on ending the war, even though neither side shows signs of backing down from their key demands. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, speaking in Helsinki on Wednesday, said Kyiv “will never accept any formula at the cost of our sovereignty or territorial integrity.” Talks between delegations from Ukraine, Russia and the United States that are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in November have not yet been scheduled because Washington is awaiting developments in the Middle East, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks Tuesday that were embargoed until Wednesday. Zelenskyy said the leaders of Finland and Norway, who spoke with Putin by phone Tuesday, told him that Russia is “serious” about discussing steps to de-escalate the war. The Ukrainian president said these could include a pause in attacks targeting energy infrastructure and commercial sea traffic, further prisoner exchanges, and a discussion of formats for possible meetings at leaders’ level. The call to the Kremlin by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was surprising. European countries have sought to diplomatically isolate the Russian leader since the invasion. But since Putin’s summit with Trump in Alaska last year, Zelenskyy noted, European governments have quietly resumed contacts with Moscow at the level of national security advisers and between intelligence agencies. Zelenskyy sees U.S. disengagement with Kyiv The Iran war has depleted stocks of U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Ukraine desperately needs to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles. Ukraine is now getting an average of 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month this year — a sharp drop from delivery rates in previous years, Zelenskyy told reporters. “Imagine this: you can count on getting 150 missiles a year from America, while you have to shoot down 150 ballistic missiles a month,” he said. Patriot delivery delays appeared to be part of a trend of U.S. disengagement with Kyiv, Zelenskyy said, following disruptions in vital internet satellite links and intelligence sharing, as well as a recent Trump administration agreement to purchase Russian diesel and waive sanctions. Elsewhere, the war rages on A Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight wounded five people, including a 4-year-old, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. The jet-powered drone attack started a major fire that set alight an apartment building, private house and an industrial building, the emergency services said. In Russia, meanwhile, the Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 531 Ukrainian drones from late Tuesday through early Wednesday. Officials said apartment buildings and industrial infrastructure in two regions were targeted, injuring five people.

articles.title: Serbian police say assailant killed after attacking officer outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade
articles.summary: An assailant with knives attacked a police officer from an elite unit guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight on Wednesday, police said.
articles.body: An assailant with knives attacked a police officer from an elite unit guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade and was killed just after midnight on Wednesday, police said. Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said that police were treating the incident as a “terrorist attack” and had raised the terror threat to the highest level and stepped up police presence at key locations. He said the attacker was a minor and had two knives. He attacked the member of the Gendarmerie, shouting Allahu Akbar, or “God is great” in Arabic. Dacic added that the police officer, who was slightly wounded in the face, killed the assailant in self-defense. Police photos from the scene showed the guard’s booth outside the embassy and the area sealed off by police tape as officers in full gear stood nearby. The attacker was believed to be from the western Serbian town of Sabac, Dacic said. He said that Serbia’s security agencies had been monitoring the attacker, who he said was a supporter of the Islamic State group. Dacic said that “he kept the black flag in support of the Islamic State on his Instagram” account. Wednesday’s attack comes just days after Serbia held a key early parliamentary election on Sunday in which long-ruling former President Aleksandar Vucic was defeated by a youth-led movement after almost two years of protests against him. But Vucic and his allies still control the police as the new government is yet to be formed. Israel also held its parliamentary vote Tuesday that exit polls said produced no clear winner. In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow also wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade. The assailant was shot and killed by the officer. Israel’s embassy is located not far from the U.S. Embassy in an upscale Belgrade district. It is guarded by an elite police unit with officers armed with automatic weapons. Serbia has maintained close relations with Israel.

articles.title: Israeli forces continue West Bank raids as Hebron lockdown enters sixth day
articles.summary: UN agency expresses ‘grave concern’ in Hebron and warns of echoes of 2025 ‘Iron Wall’ operation.
articles.body:
The Israeli army has continued its incursions into Hebron as its lockdown of the occupied West Bank’s largest city entered its sixth day.

Israeli forces raided several neighbourhoods in Hebron city as well as towns across the wider governorate on Wednesday, tightening restrictions at the entrances to the city, Anadolu news agency reported.

Troops also raided the Fawwar refugee camp south of Hebron about midnight, searching several Palestinian homes.

The Israeli army carried out raids in other areas across the occupied West Bank, detaining four Palestinians in Tulkarem, the Wafa news agency reported.

Those detained included a journalist and his two brothers, alongside an officer working for the Palestinian General Intelligence Service.

In the town of Beita, south of Nablus, troops fired tear gas at protesters demonstrating against the demolition of two homes belonging to the families of two Palestinian prisoners.

A Palestinian man sustained fractures to his hand after Israeli forces beat him during an attack on the village of Yasid, north of Nablus.

In Burin village, troops raided homes and converted several into military barracks, Wafa reported.

Schools in southern Nablus have been ordered to switch to remote learning to protect students and staff.

The raids come a day after the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) expressed “grave concern” over Israel’s continued incursions into Hebron, which have displaced nearly 5,000 Palestinians, warning that “collective punishment” violates international law.

“A near-total lockdown across large parts of Hebron has severely restricted residents’ freedom of movement and their ability to access critical services,” Roland Friedrich, the director of UNRWA Affairs for the occupied West Bank, said in a post on X.

“These developments bring alarming echoes of the massive displacement witnessed in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestine refugees from Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain forcibly displaced over a year later.”

Israel’s campaign follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week. The gunmen were later killed by Israeli forces.

Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the operation to secure settler votes before Tuesday’s elections in Israel.

articles.title: Trump gave Iran a date, not measurable terms
articles.summary: Journalist Charbel A. Antoun argues that President Trump’s Iran pause lacks measurable diplomatic goals regarding uranium accounting, inspection access, and shipping protocols, potentially serving as a mere calendar delay rather than true diplomacy.
articles.body:
By Nov. 3, I expect three things not to have happened with respect to Iran.

First, Washington will not have publicly stated what should happen to the uranium last tracked by the International Atomic Energy Agency, who would verify its disposition, or what consequences Iran would face for refusing. Second, Tehran will not have scheduled International Atomic Energy Agency access to Isfahan with a specific date and identified sites. Third, the two governments will not have agreed on a reciprocal shipping arrangement, where Iran stops attacking commercial vessels and Washington boards or diverts sanctioned tankers rather than sinking them.

If none of these happens, President Trump’s Iran pause is a calendar, not diplomacy. If any of them do happen, I will gladly concede I was wrong. But as currently structured, the pause gives neither capital a public reason to move before the election.

Trump’s Oct. 8 pledge set no Iranian condition. He said the two governments were holding productive talks. He said that the blockade of Iranian ports would stay fully in force and tied his promise not to attack to the midterm calendar. He has also said strikes could follow the election.

That differs from his April pause, which he explicitly tied to Iran’s complete, immediate and safe reopening of Hormuz. This one simply asks Iran to wait and offers no stated incentive to do more.

Before Israel’s first strikes in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency estimated Iran possessed 441 kilograms of uranium enriched to up to 60 percent . In March, Director General Rafael Grossi said the agency believed a bit more than 200 kilograms remained in tunnels at Isfahan, with some at Natanz. Iran has not told the International Atomic Energy Agency what survived or where it is, and inspectors have not returned to the bombed sites.

Putting accounting first is my judgment, not settled fact. Hawks will say the deeper problem is enrichment capacity, including an Isfahan facility that apparently escaped the attacks, and the status of centrifuges. They are right that accounting alone would solve little. But Washington cannot negotiate the disposition of material it cannot locate, and capacity limits cannot be verified until both governments establish what remains. Vice President JD Vance says Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in enrichment capacity.

But “meaningful” is not measurable. And by “measurable,” I mean Washington must identify three things: the disposition it would accept for the remaining 60 percent enriched uranium; the authority responsible for verification; and the consequences if Iran refuses.

A new shipping rule would have to cost both sides something. Iran would have to stop attacking commercial vessels. Washington would board, divert or otherwise interdict sanctioned tankers rather than sinking them, except when a vessel is attacking U.S. forces or civilian shipping. In September, U.S. forces struck Iranian tankers after an attempted attack on a Navy ship. Under this rule, that option narrows.

The blockade of Iranian ports could remain — what would change is how it is enforced.

Iran will ask what it gets in return. The honest answer is very little — no sanctions relief, no end to the blockade, no recognition of its broader demands. It would get a defined process for resolving disputed incidents. That is deliberately modest. The point is to learn whether Tehran can make any verifiable commitment.

Iran has terms of its own. In New York, it reportedly demanded that the blockade be lifted, frozen assets transferred and the war ended on all fronts. Trump rejected them. The problem is not silence. It is that neither side has turned demands into a narrow first step.

Whether Tehran can take one is unclear. As I argued earlier this month, Iran has become harder to read . As of this writing, the motion to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over the New York meeting has been registered but has not reached the agenda, and the Supreme National Security Council’s secretary has said the trip was approved in advance.

None of that proves Iran cannot make a deal. But it does suggest authority in Tehran is contested, which is precisely why the pause should test whether anyone can actually deliver on a commitment.

If Washington names terms but Tehran schedules nothing, it will be impossible to tell whether the problem is unwillingness or inability. That ambiguity is precisely the problem. If Tehran schedules access and Washington names nothing, the burden shifts to the administration. Three steps would not mean peace. They would mean the pause produced the minimum for a negotiable arrangement.

Tehran may be waiting out the clock. That does not rescue the pause. It is the point. A pause that gives both sides a reason to wait is a calendar. If Iran is waiting, it will schedule nothing. If it wants a deal, scheduling access is a limited first step: it commits Iran to a date and sites, not to enrichment limits, sanctions terms or an end to the blockade.

Trump may believe force after Nov. 3 will do better than diplomacy. But military victory is an objective, not an endgame, until Washington says what it should produce.

A pause without measurable terms is not restraint. It is a calendar.

Charbel A. Antoun is a Washington-based journalist and writer specializing in U.S. foreign policy, with a focus on the Middle East and North Africa.

articles.title: Greta Thunberg’s radical turn deserves scrutiny, not applause
articles.summary: From Paris protests to Gaza flotillas, Greta Thunberg's activist shift raises unanswered questions about funding and ties to extremist movements.
articles.body: Greta Thunberg recently traveled to France to applaud the protest movement. Wearing a black-and-white scarf associated with pro-Palestinian activism, she appeared outside a high school in a Paris suburb and lent her celebrity to demonstrations marred by rioting, arson and vandalism — with authorities already putting the damage at no less than $34 million. Thunberg brought the applause. Taxpayers were left to pay for the destruction. Her appearance fits a broader pattern of increasingly radical alliances and support for extremism. Before traveling to France, Thunberg had endorsed a motion declaring that "Zionism is racism" adopted by Britain’s Green Party on Oct. 4. WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM Her radical turn has been unfolding for years. Yet in progressive circles, she remains the Mother Teresa of the activist left — a secular saint whose moral authority is taken for granted and whose political judgment rarely faces scrutiny. As a Swede, I watched Thunberg join ABBA, Volvo and IKEA among my country’s most celebrated exports. Political leaders welcomed her. International institutions handed her a microphone. Much of the liberal media mistook her indignation for insight. She addressed parliaments, collected international prizes and was even touted for the Nobel Peace Prize. The world’s elites welcomed her criticism — and seemed rather pleased to be seen listening. The schoolgirl became a full-time activist and a political force. Her immunity from scrutiny survived the transition. From Climate Saint to Useful Idiot As Gaza moved to the center of the progressive agenda, the climate movement’s global poster child became an increasingly vocal campaigner against Israel. Her endorsement of the "Zionism is racism" motion shows how far that shift has gone. Criticizing Israeli government policies is one thing. Denying Jews the right to self-determination is another. The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism — endorsed by the United States and 42 other countries — lists denying that right, including by depicting Israel’s very existence as racist, among its examples of Jew-hatred. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Her choice of allies raises further questions. In Stockholm, Thunberg accepted an award from the Union of Palestinian Communities and Institutions in Europe — an organization that sent condolences to Hamas following the killing of its leader, Ismail Haniyeh. The representatives presenting the award wore scarves bearing the emblem of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), a Marxist-Leninist terrorist organization whose armed wing participated in the Oct. 7 attacks. Those questions followed her to sea. She joined two Gaza-bound missions and was detained and deported by Israel. Israeli authorities accused flotilla organizers of links to Hamas — allegations Thunberg rejected. Follow the Money Financial disclosures published by the Stockholm-based Greta Thunberg Foundation put its cumulative receipts and donations of award and prize money at approximately $1.3 million as of October 2025. Donations and royalties cover operating expenses, according to the foundation, which states that it does not pay Thunberg. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Meanwhile, her reported personal taxable income for 2024 was roughly $7,000. That figure alone does not explain how her globe-trotting activism is financed. Who pays for her travel, logistics and organizing? Who funds the publicity and campaign machinery behind her activism? Thunberg must answer those questions as readily as she demands answers from governments and corporations. Celebrity Is No Defense From France to Gaza, Thunberg increasingly resembles a conflict influencer: confrontation supplies the platform, and indignation over the cause du jour supplies the brand. Whatever the cause, Greta Thunberg takes center stage. It looks less and less like solidarity and more like narcissism dressed as a political cause. For a conflict influencer, peace and coexistence make poor content. Confrontation keeps the cameras rolling — and Greta in the frame. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Until she answers who funds her campaigns, what she stands for beyond slogans and why she embraces movements shadowed by extremism while preaching morality to democracies, her claim to be a voice of conscience rings hollow. She is a warning — to my country and to the world.

articles.title: Russia-Africa Summit: What is on the agenda, and why does it matter?
articles.summary: Moscow aims to strengthen economic and security ties with African leaders during the two-day gathering.
articles.body:
Trade and security are expected to be on the agenda as delegations and leaders from dozens of African countries gather in Moscow for a two-day summit with Russia.

The third instalment of the Russia-Africa Summit will run through October 28–29 and will be chaired by Russian President Vladimir Putin and the current African Union chair, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye.

Russia has boosted security and trade cooperation with African nations as it grapples with Western sanctions imposed in response to its war against Ukraine.

So who will be attending and what is at stake?

The Russia-Africa Summit is a two-day diplomatic and economic meeting being held in Moscow on Wednesday and Thursday.

Leaders and delegations from 48 African countries are meeting to discuss bilateral cooperation spanning politics, defence and technology.

This high-profile forum is the third of its kind. The first summit took place in October 2019 in Sochi, marking an unprecedented turn in Russian-African relations.

The event’s official theme is Developing Mutually Beneficial Cooperation and “unlocking the potential of every African country”.

More than 40 sessions and about 100 speakers will cover trade, investment, technology transfer, food and energy security, healthcare, education and youth exchange.

There will also be a business programme, culminating in a plenary session.

Representatives from 48 African countries will participate, as well as 22 heads of state, according to Kremlin presidential aide Yury Ushakov. Heads of state from 17 countries attended the last summit in 2023.

Fewer leaders came to the last two summits, compared with the first gathering in 2019, when 43 took part, a decline which Moscow blamed on Western pressure.

Russian President Putin is scheduled to meet with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

The guest list includes leaders closely tied to Russia’s growing security role in Africa, including Burkina Faso ’s Ibrahim Traore and Niger ’s Abdourahamane Tchiani.

Kenya’s William Ruto, Uganda’s Yoweri Museveni and Namibia’s Netumbo Nandi-Ndatiwah are also expected, as well as Sudan’s Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed al-Menfi, the chairman of the Presidential Council of Libya.

What is the relationship between Russia and Africa like?

Russia has gained far more influence in Africa through security than trade, according to a report by the African Security Analysis group (ASA), a security consultancy.

Russia’s security presence has risen significantly in the region. In 2023, Russian forces, mostly from the Wagner Group, operated in only a few African countries, but the ASA now counts Russian missions or troops in at least nine countries.

Trade between African countries and Russia has exceeded $28bn. It was estimated to be about $16.8bn in 2019, when the first summit was held. But trade is mainly concentrated in a few countries and overshadowed by that of China and the European Union.

Russia’s strongest ties to the continent are in energy, fertilisers, defence and nuclear power , where the state-owned firm Rosatom has signed a string of agreements.

Russia has been an essential supplier of fertilisers and wheat to many countries in the region.

In 2023, Russia exported 200,000 tonnes of grain to Mali, Somalia, the Central African Republic, Burkina Faso, Eritrea and Zimbabwe.

This is the first summit since 2023, so it will be an indicator of how far the relationship has developed and where it is heading, analysts say.

A final declaration and a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum plan should be adopted by the end of the Summit to cover 2027-2029.

Analysts have said that meetings on the sidelines could be more important than the main event, as talks between African delegations and Russian defence officials can illustrate where Moscow plans to expand its military ties.

The recruitment of Africans to fight in Ukraine could also be a growing problem for Moscow, as it has already caused diplomatic concern in countries such as Kenya.

Amnesty International has used the run-up to the summit to raise the issue of Africans being recruited to fight with Russia.

In an open letter , the directors of Amnesty’s African section urged leaders attending the summit to demand that Moscow end what the group describes as deceptive and coercive recruitment of Africans to fight in its war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Families brace for a fourth winter of wind, rain and floods in Gaza’s camps
articles.summary: Gaza’s impending winter is likely to lead to further devastation for Palestinians.
articles.body:
Gaza City — Mohammed al-Jamal, 60, tries to secure the nylon sheets of his family’s worn-out tent as a storm approaches his displacement camp on a beach in western Gaza City.

He and his sons pull at the tarpaulin, trying to fasten it firmly to the ground for protection from rain and wind coming in from the sea.

This will be the fourth winter that displaced Palestinians in Gaza have faced without adequate shelter. Many still live in tents and makeshift structures that offer little protection against the impending winter weather when temperatures can drop to 7C (below 45F) but can feel much colder due to strong coastal winds and rain.

The family cannot afford to fix their damaged tent with a replacement tarpaulin costing between 120 and 150 shekels ($37-$47) in local markets.

All al-Jamal can do is patch up the damaged shelter and hope it holds through the coming storm.

“We are trying to prepare as much as we can to protect ourselves from the water and the wind,” he said. “We follow the weather reports, and whenever there is a warning of a storm, we start preparing. But once the storm comes, everything gets torn apart, and we have to start all over again. It is continuous suffering throughout the winter.”

Al-Jamal, originally from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood, has been displaced several times since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

About 30 members of his extended family live in these difficult living conditions.

“We are just trying to adapt to what we have. This is what is available to us. We need everything,” he said.

When it rains, water enters the tent and floods their living space, risking damage to their meagre belongings.

When temperatures drop, tents offer little protection for the displaced, with al-Jamal and his family having no choice but to put on more layers of clothing.

“We are out in the open. We are living in the street, not in houses that protect us,” he said.

Al-Jamal said he had repeatedly heard promises that shelter materials and caravans would be allowed into Gaza, but none had arrived for his family, and he had not seen any of them enter.

He described these announcements as “false promises and lies” that had left displaced families waiting for help that never came.

“Our demand is to have our lives back the way they were before,” he said.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians and destroyed or damaged more than 80 percent of buildings. With homes and infrastructure in Gaza destroyed, about 1.5 million of Gaza’s 2.3 million people are living in tents or makeshift shelters.

Many of the displaced have been forced to move from city to city when Israeli assaults begin on their homes or camps.

At least 294,250 families in Gaza need winter shelter assistance, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), but with current supplies, only 52,000 families, roughly 18 percent of those in need, have access to partial humanitarian assistance.

More than 65 percent of displaced households were living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to a Shelter Cluster survey, with more than half of those shelters in poor or very poor condition.

Israel’s siege on Gaza has also affected supplies reaching the enclave, with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) saying on October 5 that at least 500 truckloads of shelter materials were awaiting entry or procurement.

At the current pace, NRC said, it could take more than seven months for those supplies to enter Gaza. The materials include tents, tarpaulins, ropes and other items needed to repair shelters.

For families already living in torn tents, the shortage leaves few options beyond repeatedly repairing the same shelters.

Khitam Salman, 39, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, has been displaced multiple times over the past two years.

Now living near the beach, she is trying to prepare for winter with tents that have already suffered repeated damage.

“Every time there is a storm, we put up the tarpaulins and tie them down, only to have to do it all over again,” she said. “With every low-pressure system, it is the same.”

Khitam said one of the family’s tents had collapsed four times while they were sleeping inside and was torn, allowing sand to enter and offering little protection from rain and wind.

She is trying to cover the family’s tents and the space where they store their belongings, but the costs are beyond their means.

“We need a tarpaulin for this tent, another for the other one, and one for the room where we keep our belongings,” she said. “But we don’t have the means. We have done what we can.”

Her husband works in the health sector, but she said he receives his salary only once every three months, and it is not enough to cover the family’s needs.

“The tents are not suitable for living in any more,” she said. “They are torn, and sand gets inside. It is exhausting.”

Last winter, after their tent collapsed and their belongings were soaked, Salman said she became so overwhelmed that she walked away and sat by the sea for hours.

“I was so frustrated,” she recalled. “The tent had fallen, everything was flooded, and all our belongings were wet.”

“I’m worried about this winter … that the whole nightmare will repeat itself all over again.”

Damaged roads, drainage and sewage systems also increase the risk that rainwater will mix with wastewater and swamp the camps.

Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for Gaza Municipality, said more than 85 percent of the city’s infrastructure had been damaged and its rainwater drainage system was operating at about 20 percent of its previous capacity.

Rubble, damaged drainage networks and shortages of heavy machinery, fuel and maintenance materials are hampering preparations for winter, Muhanna said.

The municipality has begun emergency cleaning and maintenance work, but its efforts remain constrained by a lack of resources.

Yosra Mesleh, 45, was displaced from her home in Gaza City’s Nassr neighbourhood when her home was destroyed and is preparing for her second winter living in a tent.

Preparing for winter means thinking about what to do when water enters their tents and soaks bedding and belongings. When this happens, they often have nowhere dry to sit, cook or eat.

“When it rained last winter, the water came inside and reached the bedding. Everything got wet,” she said. “It was difficult to find somewhere to sit while we waited for everything to dry.”

In summer, the heat and humidity inside the tent were unbearable, she said, with water shortages compounding their dire living situation.

“The place where we are living is not healthy or safe. It is not suitable for summer or winter,” she said.

Her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war, while her son is struggling to cover his own expenses.

“We need tents and tarpaulins. We need cooking utensils and a proper place to prepare food. We also need a regular supply of gas,” she said.

Without cooking gas, she worries about how the family will prepare meals when rain keeps them inside.

She remembers life before the war, when life was hard but they had an apartment and her husband ran a tea and coffee shop. They have since lost their home and their only source of income.

“We are not asking for towers or anything extravagant,” she said. “We are asking for tarpaulins and tents, for a dignified life.”

articles.title: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at U.K. rape and sex assault trial
articles.summary: Actor-comedian Russell Brand said “today is the day for truth and justice” as he arrived at a London court Wednesday to deny charges of rape and sexual assault.
articles.body: LONDON — Actor-comedian Russell Brand said “today is the day for truth and justice” as he arrived at a London court Wednesday to deny charges of rape and sexual assault. Brand spoke briefly to reporters as he entered Southwark Crown Court alongside his wife, Laura Brand. Brand, 51, stood in the witness box and took the oath, then gave his full name: Russell Edward Brand. He answered “no” to each of the charges: three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault. Questioned by his lawyer, Ian Winter, Brand said the allegations had a “devastating” impact. “My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said. Over the past two weeks of the trial, prosecutors have set out their case and the jury heard from six women who accuse Brand of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors that Brand was “ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator.” Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry. In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

images.caption: Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at court ahead of his trial, where he faces rape and sexual assault charges at Southwark Crown Court on October 28, 2026 in London, England.

articles.title: ‘Back away from this podium’: UN ambassador posts video of confrontation with Cuban reps in General Assembly Hall
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz on Tuesday posted a video depicting a confrontation between U.S. and Cuban officials while he spoke at the podium of the U.N. General Assembly chamber. The video shows Cuban officials standing and speaking to Waltz, who can be heard saying one of them needs “to back away…
articles.body:
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz on Tuesday posted a video depicting a confrontation between U.S. and Cuban officials while he spoke at the podium of the U.N. General Assembly chamber.

The video shows Cuban officials standing and speaking to Waltz, who can be heard saying one of them needs “to back away from this podium.”

“He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners,” the audio continues, with Waltz yelling, “and I’m the representative of the United States of America. Back up!”

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez is then heard raising his voice back at the former national security adviser, “You are a liar!”

More shouts are heard before Waltz urges the delegation to “please sit down. Bye. Sit down.”

Waltz later wrote in a post to the social platform X , where he shared the video, that Cuban officials can “think again about trying that nonsense in the United States of America.”

“The Castro regime has profited at the expense of the Cuban people with luxury cars, expensive watches and a private island resort,” Waltz wrote. “As I shared this with the world, regime thugs rushed the stage to interrupt my speech.”

He also shared several more videos to X of his speech blasting the Cuban regime , with one post accusing the “so called ‘diplomats'” of “melting down at the first hint of criticism in the middle of the UN.” He again compared it to “what happens to those who speak out under the iron fist of the Cuban regime at home in Havana.”

Rodríguez wrote on X that Waltz “forgets that he is at the United Nations, not at the US National Security Council, nor in a Green Berets unit, nor in a Signal group, where he has repeatedly shown his incompetence and incapacity.”

“The US government, with its crude lies at the General Assembly of the United Nations, launched a new desperate attempt to justify the economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy siege. … There is no pretext for sustaining the act of collective punishment to which they subject the Cuban people,” the foreign minister added.

The break from diplomatic decorum in the meeting place of the international body comes after months of rising tensions between the two nations.

President Trump has sought to pressure Cuba’s government to change after delivering crushing sanctions and imposing a blockade on energy into the island country. The actions led to debilitating conditions and massive power outages.

Trump administration officials and their allies have warned that Cuba’s regime would be the next to fall after the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.

The late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) said days after the conflict with the Iranian regime started that Cuba was “next.”

“Well, the truth is Cuba has already fallen ,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News’s Sean Hannity last month. “It does not have a functional economy, and it is governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years. It’s never worked.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s energy strategy is built for Russia’s attacks but not global shocks
articles.summary: As Ukraine prepares for another winter under Russian attacks, its energy strategy is undergoing a fundamental transformation.
articles.body:
As Ukraine prepares for another winter under Russian attacks, its energy strategy is undergoing a fundamental transformation. Large power plants and centralized networks remain essential, but cities are increasingly turning to distributed generation: gas-fired units, cogeneration, modular boiler houses, solar panels, batteries and backup generators.

The logic is clear. A single missile strike can disable a large power facility, while hundreds of smaller sources spread across a city are harder to eliminate at once.

Ukraine’s government has made distributed generation and decentralized heating central elements of its resilience plans for the upcoming winter. More than $1.4 billion has been allocated for these plans, with another $210 million coming from local budgets.

But decentralization should not be confused with energy independence.

Ukraine may become less dependent on a centralized electricity grid while becoming more dependent on fuel, gas infrastructure, imported equipment and global energy markets. That distinction matters especially now, as the war between the U.S. and Iran has increased volatility in international energy markets.

Ukraine’s dependence on imported petroleum products is already significant. Wartime destruction of domestic refining capacity has forced the country to rely heavily on imports , with Lithuania accounting for about 32 percent of fuel imports in September and Poland for another 25 percent, followed by suppliers including Germany, Romania and Greece.

That creates a paradox. A diesel generator can protect a hospital, water utility or heating system when the grid fails. But the generator itself depends on a reliable supply of diesel. If international fuel prices rise or shipping becomes more expensive, the cost of maintaining that local resilience rises as well.

The same problem applies to gas-fired generation, which Ukraine is expanding rapidly. As of July, approximately 1.8 gigawatts of distributed gas-fired generation had been installed across the country. The Kyiv region alone accounted for more than 219 megawatts.

Gas generation reduces dependence on vulnerable centralized power plants, but it does not eliminate infrastructure dependencies. Every new facility still needs a functioning gas distribution network, adequate capacity, technical connections and reliable fuel supplies.

In 2026, Gas Distribution Networks of Ukraine reported connecting 140 distributed generation facilities , with another 86 planned by the end of the year. Each project requires network capacity assessment, design, construction, connection and gas commissioning. This is why municipal capacity is becoming as important as physical equipment.

Ukraine’s winter resilience plans recognize this problem. The government says more than 2,500 boiler houses and nearly 3,000 kilometers of heating networks have been prepared for the 2026-27 season, while $110 million has been allocated specifically for distributed heat generation.

Yet cities do not enter winter with equal resources or administrative capacity. Some can quickly procure equipment, secure international financing and complete complex infrastructure projects. Others struggle with project design, procurement, grid or gas connections and maintenance.

Recent developments in Kyiv illustrate the problem. On Oct. 11, Ukraine’s Energy Ministry ordered authorities to accelerate the installation and connection of distributed generation facilities in the capital, citing continued Russian attacks on energy equipment and high-voltage networks. Now the global energy market adds another layer of risk.

The U.S.-Iran war and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed Brent crude above $100 per barrel and increased concerns about diesel supplies, shipping costs and insurance premiums. On Oct. 21 , Brent was trading around $109 per barrel, while attacks on shipping in and around Hormuz continued.

For Ukraine, this matters even if the fuel never comes directly from the Middle East. Higher global oil prices affect European fuel markets, transport costs and the price Ukraine pays for imported diesel and other petroleum products.

The lesson is not that Ukraine should abandon distributed generation. Quite the opposite. Decentralization is essential to surviving Russia’s campaign against the energy system. But Ukraine and its international partners should think beyond simply delivering generators.

The next generation of resilience should combine distributed generation with energy storage, renewable sources, diversified fuel supplies, efficient local heating systems and stronger municipal technical capacity. International assistance should help communities finance not only equipment, but also engineering, connection, maintenance, fuel planning and project management.

Ukraine is trying to escape the vulnerability created by a centralized energy system. The challenge now is to ensure that it does not replace one dependency with another.

For the U.S. and its allies, that should be a central lesson of Ukraine’s wartime energy transformation: Resilience is not simply the ability to generate electricity locally. It is the ability to keep generating it when the next shock comes from somewhere else.

Kateryna Odarchenko is president of the PolitA Institute for Democracy and Development, a political consultant, a partner of the SIC Group Ukraine and a member of the International Association of Political Consultants.

articles.title: Lula is an uncomfortable but necessary trading partner
articles.summary: The relationship with Brazil will require a twofold effort: to contain Chinese expansion and to negotiate with an awkward, unreliable — yet inevitably necessary — partner.
articles.body:
On Oct. 25, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva became president of Brazil for the fourth time. After a first-round defeat, he made a radical comeback and won the election with 51.8 percent over his rival, President Trump’s ally Flávio Bolsonaro, who reached 48.2 percent. That’s a difference of more than 4 million votes.

Following his victory, Lula stated that Brazil “will not accept being anyone’s backyard.” The next day, President Trump said it “looked like another rigged election.” Despite this, the two presidents have met three times over the last 13 months — not out of ideological affinity, but rather for the sake of commercial pragmatism.

In 2025 , U.S. goods and services trade with Brazil totaled $135.7 billion, up 6.5 percent from 2024. The U.S. is Brazil’s second-largest trading partner . Both countries need each other, beyond the huge ideological differences.

President Trump said : “I’m not running Brazil, I’m running the USA. I like Lula, I get along with him pretty well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated.”

Lula and Trump represent opposite poles. While the U.S. president comes from the private sector, Lula was a labor leader who, for more than 50 years, fought against the private sector. He is a classic 20th-century leftist leader, friend of dictators like Fidel Castro in Cuba and Daniel Ortega in Nicaragua. He knows the populist playbook and knows how to use it.

His electoral victory came with a huge price tag. The leader of the Worker’s Party pushed for at least $57 billion for a massive social program expansion, covering everything from debt relief packages for small business owners to family subsidies for food, gas prices, credit card forgiveness and more.

Yes, Lula won the election, but the next day Brazil currency plunged to a historic 11 percent over the dollar, the lowest record reported in decades, while stock markets panicked and closed down 14 percent.

Beyond Lula’s victory, Brazil continues to be the largest country in Latin America and one of largest democracies in the world. The country will continue to be part of the G20 and the so-called Global South within the BRICS group, which includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It’s a pivotal player with strategic relations with both Western democracies and authoritarian regimes.

Lula’s victory marks a challenge for the new Monroe Doctrine after seven electoral victories in Latin American countries. However, while confronting Brazil is not good for business, ignoring its dangerous alignment with U.S. extra regional adversaries could be a massive mistake.

Lula’s alliance with China goes beyond the traditional trade relations. Earlier this year, Brazil received the military hospital ship Silk Road Ark owned by the People’s Liberation Army Navy. The countries’ naval forces conducted a joint maritime exercise on search and rescue. China also made a demonstration of a combat and rescue operation.

The Brazilian president has opened the door to China’s biggest companies, including electric car company BYD and Huawei, a telecom giant accused of espionage by several European countries and the United States.

Lula has also maintained a critical distance from the “Shield of the Americas,” the U.S. flagship security alliance in the Western hemisphere. Brazil has also refused to designate criminal gangs like the Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho as terrorist organizations.

The recent electoral results in Brazil were not as expected, but they represent a stark reality. The South American nation will be governed for another four years by a strong anti-American socialist — a friend to China, Russia and Iran, as well as defender of the dictatorships of Cuba and Nicaragua. Yet it is also a trading giant that is vital to the United States.

The relationship with Brazil will require a twofold effort: to contain Chinese expansion and to negotiate with an awkward, unreliable — yet inevitably necessary — partner.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.title: Photos: Spain high-speed train crash kills 30
articles.summary: Health Minister Monica Garcia says emergency workers are focusing on rescuing survivors.
articles.body:
A high-speed train has slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two carriages in central Spain and killing at least 30 people, authorities have said.

At least 80 people were injured in the crash that occurred early on Wednesday near Urda, in Toledo province, south of Madrid, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano Garcia-Page, said, warning that the death toll could rise.

Spain’s Health Minister Monica Garcia said emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and recovering bodies from the two most damaged carriages. She said the injured were being taken to several hospitals in the area.

In January, 45 people were killed in southern Spain when a train left the tracks and collided with an oncoming service. That crash was Spain’s deadliest since 2013, when 80 people were killed in a derailment.

articles.title: Government minister McAllan calls for review of 'unacceptable' BBC Scotland channel closure
articles.summary: The BBC announced the dedicated Scotland channel would move online as part of measures to make savings of £500m.
articles.body:
Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan has urged Ofcom to review "wholly unacceptable" plans to close the linear BBC Scotland channel.

The BBC last week announced the dedicated Scotland channel - as well as BBC Three and Radio 4 Extra - would move online as part of measures to make £500m of savings by 2028.

McAllan said moving the channel online would "reverse progress in improving the visibility and representation of Scotland within the UK's broadcasting landscape".

She called on Ofcom, the UK's independent broadcasting regulator, to scrutinise the decision and its implications.

McAllan wrote: "The Scottish government considers the proposed closure of the linear BBC Scotland channel to be wholly unacceptable, and we oppose such a move in the strongest possible terms."

BBC Scotland TV channel to close amid cuts to services

In the letter, to the watchdog's chief executive Melanie Dawes and director for Scotland Glenn Preston, McAllan said she understood that broadcasters must adapt to evolve with audience habits.

But she added public service broadcasters had a "unique responsibility to ensure their services remain accessible and relevant".

McAllan continued: "Closure of the linear channel would also be impossible to reconcile with a supposed ambition to move power and decision-making away from London and towards audiences across the UK who are paying for the service.

"Many viewers continue to rely on linear television services, and any move away from those services risks disproportionately affecting audiences who are less likely to access content through online platforms."

The culture secretary added that plans to close the nightly News at Seven programme would be a "totally unacceptable reduction in nationally relevant journalism".

The closure of the programme is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year.

McAllan also called out a "disparity in indigenous language broadcasting" and highlighted the "total absence" of Commonwealth Games coverage on BBC One Scotland.

The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.

Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.

The current plans won't see any changes to BBC Scotland's main news programme Reporting Scotland, which is shown on BBC One or the broadcasters radio or online services.

After the announcement, Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine said more cuts could be on the way.

The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.

In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.

In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus.

Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.

The broadcaster, which has about 21,500 full time employees, gets most of its income from the licence fee, but the number of TV licences sold has been declining in recent years.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "While decisions about closing a service are a matter for the BBC Board, Ofcom's role is to hold the BBC to account for delivering its mission and public purposes.

"We will be engaging with the BBC to understand how it plans to serve audiences across the UK in light of its proposed changes and will respond to the cabinet secretary in due course."

As a public service broadcaster, the BBC's mission is "to act in the public interest, serving all audiences through the provision of impartial, high-quality and distinctive output and services which inform, educate and entertain".

articles.title: Trump says he approves of Bolsonaro coming to US
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday said he approves of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro entering the U.S. after his runoff election loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva earlier this week. “Well, I would approve,” Trump told reporters outside Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews. “I think they’re fine people. The election was…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday said he approves of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro entering the U.S. after his runoff election loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva earlier this week.

“Well, I would approve,” Trump told reporters outside Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews. “I think they’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It got bad reviews, and look what happened to their market.”

Trump added that he “didn’t take sides” and that he knows “Flávio a little bit” and Bolsonaro’s father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing leader compared to his U.S. counterpart as the “Trump of the tropics.”

Trump told reporters that he had heard the younger Bolsonaro was in Argentina. The candidate fled to Argentina and then Ecuador before the Trump administration granted Bolsonaro and his family visas to enter the U.S.

The State Department aimed to tilt Brazil’s election in favor of Bolsonaro in the lead-up to the election, Reuters reported .

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and barred him from leaving the country, The Guardian reported . The order stems from an investigation into Bolsonaro for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo, said his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.

Bolsonaro lost to Lula as the president won an unprecedented fourth term. He and the incumbent requested Brazil’s electoral court to extend the election for two hours, both citing issues preventing voters from getting to the polls.

Bolsonaro called for the election’s results to be annulled and has not verbally conceded, though his Liberal Party accepted defeat on Monday. The Brazilian outlet Folha de S.Paulo reported that allies urged Bolsonaro to drop his calls for the results to be annulled.

Speaking from the capital Brasília, Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, said Bolsonaro should have remained in the country to prove his innocence in connection with the investigation.

“This act of leaving Brazil is shameful,” Lula told supporters, according to Reuters . “When I was asked to surrender my passport, I did so. He should have done the same. If the Federal Police suspected he was going to leave Brazil, he ought to have surrendered his. Regrettably, that is the Bolsonaro family for you.”

Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a postelection coup in 2022 before Lula returned to power, having previously served as president from 2003 to 2011.

Lula’s passport was seized in 2017 amid an investigation into the country’s massive Lava Jato, or “Operation Car Wash,” corruption scandal. The then-former president surrendered to federal authorities and was charged in connection with the scandal.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Edson Fachin overturned Lula’s nine-year conviction in 2021, allowing Lula to seek office again and become a vocal critic against Bolsonaro’s father.

articles.title: Around the world, voters are embracing democracy
articles.summary: With rising gas and cost-of-living prices, war in Iran, corruption in the White House, AI’s threat to the job market and energy-guzzling data centers warming the planet, Americans may well be on the cusp of demanding radical change.
articles.body:
Galvanized by youth movements in Serbia and Brazil, voters over the weekend came out in droves to register their choice for democracy over authoritarianism. The dual outpouring of democratic agency should make clear to a frightened American populace that the end of the free world is far from inevitable.

American voters must follow the lead of Serbians and Brazilians when they head to the polls for the midterm elections next week by making clear to those in power that the fate of the nation depends not on the whims of billionaire oligarchs or the faint courage of Democrats in Congress. It depends on the will of the American people.

It took barely two years for students in Serbia to successfully spearhead a powerful movement to bring down president Aleksandar Vucic’s twelve-year government, which was plagued by negligence and corruption. The swell began on Nov. 1, 2024, when a concrete roof jutting from the primary railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, collapsed, killing sixteen people. The tragedy triggered a national campaign against Vucic that started with weekly protests by students on university campuses but grew into rallies and door-to-door campaigns behind a slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?”

The leaderless student effort became a national movement capturing numerous segments of Serbian society — including farmers, teachers, actors and lawyers. It culminated in the country’s largest anti-government protest in March 2025 in Belgrade, and later, a demand for early parliamentary elections. Vucic finally announced snap elections in September, claiming the protestors were trying to “bring down” Serbia with the support of “the American deep state.” Turnout was historic, topping 67.6 percent as of Sunday evening local time, the highest since Yugoslavia’s breakup in 1992.

Brazil’s democracy dates back to 1985, following a 21-year military dictatorship. Like their counterparts in Serbia, Brazil’s youth drove a grassroots campaign – one that capitalized on coordinated messaging across digital media. As a result, the 80-year-old incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, defeated the right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro , son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The elder Bolsonaro had refused to accept his own loss to Lula in 2022 and was later sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup to illegally stay in power.

Lula’s 52 percent victory amid 80 percent turnout was stunning, as it came after he had lost to Bolsonaro in the first-round election by over two million votes. The younger Bolsonaro has fled the country . The U.S. State Department issued him a visa after a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered that he surrender his passport as part of a money laundering investigation, and Trump called the election “rigged.”

These latest victories for liberal democracy come on the heels of Viktor Orban’s historic defeat six months ago in his bid to continue as leader of Hungary. Public opposition to Orban’s stints as prime minister, which ran from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010 to 2026, began in earnest in 2024 after his government pardoned a former director of a children’s home who had been convicted of covering up sexual abuse.

As in Serbia and Brazil, Hungarian youth were at the forefront of ultimately toppling the far-right regime. In 2022, high school students helped stage a 35,000-person protest against Orban’s education policy before the Budapest Parliament, chanting “No teachers, no future.”

Americans are increasingly disillusioned with their own 250-year-old democracy, and for good reason. President Trump’s approval rating is near record lows just a week ahead of the midterms. A whopping 73 percent of recent poll respondents disapprove of his handling of fuel prices; 52 percent said they plan to vote for a Democratic candidate next month.

The popularity of American democracy itself isn’t faring much better. A Kettering-Gallup study from September revealed that only 19 percent of American adults believe that U.S. democracy is performing well; 56 percent said it is doing poorly. According to a poll released by Harvard in October, a staggering 91 percent of voters say the U.S. is on the wrong track. According to another Gallup poll , the “thriving” rate for Americans aged 18-20 fell 20 percentage points from 2020 to early 2026, to just 44 percent, with only 49 percent of young people expecting a high-quality life in five years.

With rising gas and cost-of-living prices, Trump’s meaningless war in Iran, abject corruption in the White House, artificial intelligence’s threat to the job market and Silicon Valley’s energy-guzzling data centers warming the planet at exponential rates, Americans may well be on the cusp of demanding radical change.

As the elections in Hungary, Serbia and Brazil seem to show, the way to make change is to vote — and to do so in exceptionally huge numbers, not at the typical 40 percent eligible-voter turnout rate for U.S. midterm elections. For Americans still inclined to stay home, the lesson is simple: Authoritarianism thrives when ordinary people conclude that their voices no longer matter.

If adult voters won’t do it for their own sake, perhaps they will think of the daunting odds stacked against our children and make a bet that their futures will still be bright.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a thematic group coordinator and fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: Look of the Week: It’s Drake’s birthday and he’ll wear red leather pants if he wants to
articles.summary: Drake appeared over the weekend in a series of over-the-top birthday outfits that seemed to relay a clear message: new decade, new Drake.
articles.body: If you were a polarizing Canadian rapper who had a tumultuous end to your 30s and had spent the better part of the last year releasing a trove of new music to change the narrative, what would you want to signal through your 40th birthday attire? Drake, who turned 40 on Saturday, appeared this weekend in a series of over-the-top outfits that seemed to relay a message: new decade, new Drake. And while he’s always favored a big coat, a cozy knit or, better yet, a big and cozy knit, the new tenets of his style seem to highlight his tendencies toward, maximalist, playful and sometimes absurd pairings. His big brown poncho, or as The Cut dubbed it, his “Christian Girl Autumn” look, went viral so quickly that it generated Halloween costume inspiration in less than a day. But then he followed it up with this: a custom Chrome Hearts faux-fur leopard print jacket emblazoned with red crosses, a flowy white dress shirt, matching slick red leather pants and burgundy cowboy boots. The look also had a subtle, sentimental touch; he wore a portrait of his parents housed inside a custom Anomaly Relic necklace gifted to him by his stylist, Juliet Charlotte. She also confirmed she’s the one behind his full set of birthday outfits. Turning 40 is a big milestone for anyone, especially for people with no shortage of funds to do strange or extravagant things to stave off a mid-life crises. Grace Kelly famously threw a lavish Scorpio party, Beyoncé launched an interactive website and Kim Kardashian hosted a private-island affair that was criticized for being tone deaf during the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic. Over the past year, Drake has seemingly wrestled with when to lay low and when to pull stunts. But for his birthday, he leaned into the latter, reportedly booking the Backstreet Boys for a private performance at Cipriani in New York and giving away $1 million to his guests during the party. His birthday looks set the tone of the weekend, and when it comes to public perception, you either love or hate the rapper, and the same goes for his sense of style. You almost have to admire his later-in-life embrace of kitsch. (Remember his filled-to-the-brim room of Hermès Birkins set aside for his future wife?) Though he has yet to announce dates, Drake has signaled he’ll tour next year following his three-part album release of 2026. It’ll be an opportunity for a full rebrand and a reminder that Drake is never afraid to be unapologetically, well, Drake.

articles.title: Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro arrives in Miami after election defeat
articles.summary: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his ​family arrived in Miami on Wednesday, where the United States government will grant them entry visas after he refused to comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.
articles.body: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his ​family arrived in Miami on Wednesday, where the United States government will grant them entry visas after he refused to comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s presidential election to leftist incumbent ⁠Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, left Brazil under a shroud of secrecy after the court order, which relates to a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing. Reuters TV images showed Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters disembarking from the Gulfstream G400 and heading into Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport. Their ⁠journey to the United States captured attention ​across the ⁠region. They entered northern Argentina late on Tuesday evening, according to the country’s migration department, and then took a private jet to the Ecuadorean city ⁠of Guayaquil. From there, they flew to Miami. Neither Argentina’s presidency, Ecuadorean ministries nor Baires ​Fly, the ⁠operator of the private jet, ‌responded to requests for comment. Lula condemns departure “I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula told supporters Wednesday. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.” Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement he couldn’t confirm information from foreign authorities but that “Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family.” Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, earlier said he hadn’t spoken to the defeated candidate since early Tuesday morning. “We had no news from Flávio or his lawyers about what happened,” Marinho said. “I received a text message from him, he said he wanted to take a break and then he would talk to us. That’s the only message I had from him.” Brazilian media reported many Bolsonaro allies were unable to reach him. Fresh Brazil-U.S. rift Bolsonaro’s departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with ‌the Bolsonaro family to help return them to power. ‌Ahead of Sunday’s election, Reuters reported on a US State Department campaign to restore the Bolsonaros to office. Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the United States, after his State Department ⁠said it would give them entry visas. Trump has previously alleged that Flávio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. Jair Bolsonaro also travelled to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022, during Joe Biden’s presidency. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia. Flávio Bolsonaro had ‌been widely expected to win Sunday’s election but suffered a shock defeat. Bolsonaro, ​who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in ‌February, had said on Monday after ⁠the order to hand in his passports that he had no plans to ⁠flee. “I have never thought about leaving the country,” he said. “I will hand over my passports and ‌defend myself against this travesty, ​which is a clear attempt to intimidate ‌me.”

articles.title: Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing Daily Mail journalists
articles.summary: The 43-year-old is convicted after a week-long trial at Southwark Crown Court.
articles.body:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has been convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found the 43-year-old, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.

The court had heard how Robinson, from Bedfordshire, used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, forcing them to employ security or leave home.

Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He told the jury he felt the article had "endangered" his family by revealing they were staying in a hotel near Ayia Napa in Cyprus.

After the guilty verdicts, Frank Ferguson, the head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Robinson had "weaponised social media and subjected two journalists to a campaign of harassment which caused them serious fear of violence".​

Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 December‌.

Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, or up to 14 years if the offence is racially or religiously aggravated.

During the week-long trial, prosecutor Ben Holt had told the court that after three girls were murdered in Southport on 29 July 2024, Robinson had made a number of posts on social media. This had alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.

The Daily Mail published articles with photos of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".

Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he responded with a series of posts on his X account.

On 4 August, these had included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."

Robinson admitted hiring private investigators to take photographs of the home addresses of Dirnhuber and Young.

He said he had "wanted to find the journalists" to "put pressure on them".

But he told the jury he had not known they were "in fear."

"That wasn't my intention at all," he said.

"It was an attempt to bring the Daily Mail to the table."

The jury accepted the prosecution's case that Robinson had hired detectives to "intimidate" the journalists.

Photographs of Dirnhuber outside his home and cropped images of Young's family had been posted online by Robinson.

The court heard that, as well as social media posts and direct messages to Dirnhuber, the defendant had become "increasingly menacing" on a telephone call with Young on August 5, 2024, telling the freelance journalist: "I'm coming to get you."

Jurors rejected Robinson's claim that the Daily Mail had endangered his family by publishing the story.

He had wept in the witness box on Thursday as he spoke about his relationship with his children.

A police investigation had begun after the journalists reported concerns for their safety following posts on X that had contained their personal information.

A Met Police spokesperson said: "There are legitimate and established routes that can be pursued by people who have concerns or complaints about their treatment by the media."

They said, instead of following these routes, Robinson had issued "threatening online posts in the knowledge that they would almost certainly lead to his followers to target and intimidate those journalists".

The spokesperson said the journalists, fearing for their families' safety, had left their homes and hired private security.

The spokesperson added: "This kind of intimidatory behaviour is not acceptable, and anyone behaving in such a way to intimidate, harass and threaten others either online or in the real world can expect to be investigated and brought before the courts, as was the case here."

articles.summary: Epifanio Gaminde allegedly mailed his missing wife's credit cards to a relative in the Philippines to create the illusion she was alive overseas.
articles.body: A Florida man accused of murdering his missing wife allegedly sent her identification and credit cards to a relative in the Philippines as part of an elaborate effort to make it appear she was alive and living overseas, authorities said. Epifanio IX Ramos Gaminde was indicted on a first-degree murder charge in the disappearance of his wife, Maria Gaminde, whose family has had no confirmed contact with her since January 2024. Her body has not been found, but investigators searched the couple's DeBary, Florida, property Tuesday after a neighbor reported seeing Gaminde doing extensive work behind the home around the time his wife disappeared. CALIFORNIA NURSE'S HUSBAND CLAIMED ICE TOOK HER — NOW HE'S CHARGED WITH MURDER Maria's family reported her missing in January 2024 after losing contact with her. By July of that year, relatives were raising concerns with investigators about text messages, emails and credit-card activity that purportedly came from Maria overseas. "The family starts to contact us and say, 'Hey, something's not right. These text messages and emails that we're getting, the spending on her credit cards, too. Something's not right,'" Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood said during a news conference Tuesday. SISTER OF MISSING DC MOM SPEAKS OUT AFTER EX’S ARREST EXPOSES 'HORRIFYING' ABUSIVE RELATIONSHIP Gaminde told investigators the couple was having marital problems and claimed his wife had left for either the Philippines or Japan. Investigators believe the activity was intended to create the appearance that Maria was alive and avoiding contact with her family, friends and law enforcement. Authorities traced Maria's last known activity to December 2023. Investigators determined Maria and her children visited Disney World's Magic Kingdom on Dec. 16 after confirming their fingerprints were used to enter the park. ACCUSED WIFE KILLER BARRY MORPHEW BACK BEHIND BARS AFTER SEPARATE INCIDENT THAT SKYROCKETED BOND: PROSECUTORS Four days later, Gaminde allegedly sent his wife a text asking where she was. Communications from Maria then stopped before messages purportedly from her began coming from overseas. Despite those communications and the apparent activity on Maria's accounts, investigators found no evidence that she was still alive. TEXAS MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PREGNANT WIFE ALLEGEDLY CUTS OFF ANKLE MONITOR AND FLEES TO ITALY "There's no financial trail. There's nothing that would indicate that Maria is alive," Chitwood said. During Tuesday's search of the couple's property, investigators focused on an area behind the home where concrete appeared to have been added. Chitwood cautioned that investigators did not know whether the search would lead them to Maria's remains. articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after fleeing Brazil
articles.summary: Failed Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has landed in the U.S. after fleeing his home country following the election results. Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday, after the State Department extended them visas, The Associated Press reported. Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro’s passports to be returned as he was under investigation…
articles.body:
Failed Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has landed in the U.S. after fleeing his home country following the election results.

Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday, after the State Department extended them visas , The Associated Press reported.

Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro’s passports to be returned as he was under investigation for alleged financial crimes. It is unclear whether he complied with the ruling before exiting the South American nation.

The group crossed into Argentina via a bridge border crossing, Argentina’s migration authority wrote on the social platform X, and they possessed valid documentation to cross into the neighboring country “without any legal impediment.”

Bolsonaro lost the presidential runoff election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva — though he claimed the election results were fraudulent. His father, embattled former President Jair Bolsonaro, did the same after losing the 2022 election.

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a prison sentence for a postelection coup attempt.

President Trump said Tuesday that he approved of Flávio Bolsonaro and his family being allowed into the U.S., calling the election “very strange.” He previously blasted the results as “rigged” on Monday.

While the president supported the elder Bolsonaro in 2022, he did not publicly endorse a candidate in this year’s election.

Trump has often sparred with his Brazilian counterpart, more commonly known as Lula, over his tariff agenda. The U.S. president hit Brazil with 50 percent import taxes last year.

Lula later called the move politically motivated. The president did not outright deny the claim but said the tariffs were only in part due to the prosecution of the elder Bolsonaro.
